# A photo key to Montana's broadleaf trees

Montana has eleven native broadleaf (hardwood) trees, from the box
elders and green ash of the eastern river bottoms to the aspen groves
and paper birches of the mountains. This vignette shows a dichotomous
key to them, written as a plain spreadsheet with a folder of photos, and
the two ways dimoose can show it: a printable diagram and an interactive
wizard.

## Make your own key in three steps

The key is an ordinary CSV file, so the quickest way to write a key of
your own is to start from a copy of it:

1.  **Copy the template.** It ships with dimoose, next to its photos:

    ``` r

    template <- system.file("extdata", "montana", package = "dimoose")
    dir.create("~/my-key")
    file.copy(template, "~/my-key", recursive = TRUE)   # makes ~/my-key/montana/
    ```

2.  **Edit it in Excel, Numbers or Google Sheets.** One row per lead:

    | Column | What goes in it |
    |----|----|
    | `Couplet` | The couplet’s number. |
    | `Choice` | Optional: `a`, `b`, …; left blank, the leads are lettered in order. |
    | `Question` | Optional: what the couplet asks, such as “Leaf type?”. |
    | `Description` | What the lead says. |
    | `Goes to` | The next couplet, or blank when the lead names a species. |
    | `Species` | The result, written “Common name (Genus species)”. |
    | `Photo` | Optional: photo file names in the same folder, separated by `;`. |

    Put your photos in the same folder and save the sheet as CSV.

3.  **Build the key and look at it:**

    ``` r

    library(dimoose)
    k <- keyFromSpreadsheet("~/my-key/montana/montana-key.csv", desc = "My key")
    k$validate()                       # lists any couplet that is never reached, etc.
    keyDiagram(k, "my-key.svg")        # a printable diagram
    exportWizard(k, "my-key.html")     # an interactive key for phones and browsers
    ```

If a row points to a couplet that is not in the sheet, or names a photo
that is not in the folder,
[`keyFromSpreadsheet()`](https://leipzig.github.io/dimoose/reference/keyFromSpreadsheet.md)
says which spreadsheet row to fix.

## The Montana key

``` r

library(dimoose)
k <- montanaKey()
k
#> <dimoose key> Key to the native broadleaf trees of Montana
#>   10 couplets, 20 leads, 11 taxa, up to 7 steps deep
```

[`montanaKey()`](https://leipzig.github.io/dimoose/reference/exampleKeys.md)
is
[`keyFromSpreadsheet()`](https://leipzig.github.io/dimoose/reference/keyFromSpreadsheet.md)
applied to the template above. Its first rows:

``` r

csv <- system.file("extdata", "montana", "montana-key.csv", package = "dimoose")
head(read.csv(csv, check.names = FALSE), 4)
#>   Couplet Choice   Question
#> 1       1      a Leaf type?
#> 2       1      b Leaf type?
#> 3       2      a  Leaflets?
#> 4       2      b  Leaflets?
#>                                                                                  Description
#> 1                                           Leaves compound, divided into separate leaflets.
#> 2                                                             Leaves simple, a single blade.
#> 3 Leaves opposite, with 3 (rarely 5) leaflets that have a few coarse teeth or shallow lobes.
#> 4                                Leaves opposite, with 5 to 7 leaflets with toothed margins.
#>   Goes to                            Species                           Photo
#> 1       2                                    fraxinus_pennsylvanica_leaf.jpg
#> 2       3                                         populus_deltoides_leaf.jpg
#> 3      NA           Box elder (Acer negundo)           acer_negundo_leaf.jpg
#> 4      NA Green ash (Fraxinus pennsylvanica) fraxinus_pennsylvanica_leaf.jpg
```

Every species was checked as native to Montana in the [Montana Field
Guide](https://fieldguide.mt.gov) and [USDA
PLANTS](https://plants.usda.gov). Common hackberry is left out because
the Montana Field Guide gives its origin in the state as undetermined,
and American elm because it is planted rather than native. The
characters in each couplet come from the Montana Field Guide’s
descriptions and, for leaf stalks and buds, the [Virginia Tech
Dendrology](https://dendro.cnre.vt.edu) fact sheets;
[`?montana`](https://leipzig.github.io/dimoose/reference/montana.md)
lists the sources. The 14 photos are from Wikimedia Commons, most of
them taken in Montana by Matt Lavin; their authors and licenses are in
the package’s `COPYRIGHTS` file.

## A diagram of the key

[`keyDiagram()`](https://leipzig.github.io/dimoose/reference/keyDiagram.md)
draws any key top-down: each question in a blue box, its leads below it,
and each species in a green box with its photo.

``` r

keyDiagram(k, "montana-key.svg")
```

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

## An interactive key

[`exportWizard()`](https://leipzig.github.io/dimoose/reference/exportWizard.md)
writes the same key as a single web page that asks one question at a
time and shows the photos with each answer. It works offline, so it can
be copied to a phone and used in the field.

``` r

page <- tempfile(fileext = ".html")
exportWizard(k, page)
```

Open the file in a browser to try it.

## Diagrams of other keys

[`keyDiagram()`](https://leipzig.github.io/dimoose/reference/keyDiagram.md)
works on every dimoose key, whichever way it was made. Here is the key
to the orders of Arachnida, transcribed from a textbook:

``` r

keyDiagram(arachnidaKey(), "arachnida.svg")
```
